# Pre-1900 Temperature Sources: What Is Safe to Load

## 1. Survival rate and the headline number

**89 of 97 survived independent re-read. That is a 91.8 percent survival rate, an 8.2 percent loss.**

| Pass | Loss to independent re-read |
|---|---|
| Earlier passes on this project | 12 percent to 88 percent |
| This pass | 8.2 percent |

This is the cleanest pass the project has run, by a wide margin. Fourteen verifiers downloaded their own copies of every source into their own isolated directories, grepped locally, and used no file produced by another agent. Not one of the 97 quotes was fabricated. On a project that has already withdrawn eighteen citations for being invented or misattributed, that is a genuinely different result.

Be suspicious of it anyway, for two reasons. First, an unusually clean batch is exactly what a lax pass also looks like. The evidence that this one is real is that the failures the verifiers did find are the subtle kind, not the easy kind: a genuine quote pointed at the wrong plant, a genuine quote whose word turns out not to be a temperature. A lazy verifier does not find those. Second, and this matters more:

**Every verification record handed to me was truncated mid-sentence at a fixed character budget.** The "[truncated in source]" markers show where each record ended. Everything below is built on partial concern text. The untruncated records must be re-pulled before anyone acts on any of this.

**89 confirmed does not mean 89 loadable. My count of what is actually safe is 42, and every one of those still needs its citation string repaired first.** See section 5.

---

## 2. The eight rejections, and the two very different ways they failed

Split them, because they are not the same problem and only one of them is the problem this database keeps repeating.

### Failure type one: the quote is real but it is pointed at the wrong thing (5)

These are locator and scope errors. The words on the page are genuine and verbatim. They just do not belong to the row.

| ID | Herb | What actually happened |
|---|---|---|
| H151 | Common Mallow | Passage is genuine and verbatim, but it sits under "HERBS AND THEIR LEAVES" in the simples commentary of The English Physician and Family Dispensatory, not in A Catalogue of Simples in the New Dispensatory as claimed |
| H132 | Sarsaparilla | Text is exactly verbatim at Culpeper line 15824. The locator names the wrong part of the book |
| H261 | Kanchnar (Bauhinia variegata) | Locator resolves exactly, text is verbatim to the character. Wrong species or part |
| H138 | Guggul | Quoted sentence verbatim, page locator correct. Dymock is describing the different kinds of bdellium, not the row's drug |
| H299 | Cape Aloes | Gerard's chapter 141 quote is genuine and correctly located. It is "Herb Aloe or Sea Houseleek", not Aloe ferox resin |

Three of these five would have loaded a real classical temperature onto a plant that never received it.

### Failure type two: the quote is real, the plant is right, and the word is not a temperature (3)

**This is the subtler failure and the one this database keeps falling for.** In each case a verifier had to read the word in its own book-structural context and decide whether it was thermal doctrine or something else wearing thermal clothing.

| ID | Herb | The word that was not a temperature |

| H244 | Skunk Cabbage | Schöpf 1787, both printings downloaded and checked. The passage is genuinely there and correctly located under GYNANDRIA POLYANDRIA. It carries no thermal assignment |
| H105 | Prickly Ash | Thomson's entry banner reads "Antiscorbutics continued". Antiscorbutic is a therapeutic class, an action. It is not a temperature |
| H221 | Stone Root | Locator resolves precisely to the PROPERTIES block. What is in that block is actions |

The pattern to internalise: **an action list and a temperature look identical in a citation string.** "Antiscorbutic", "alterative", "tonic", "diuretic", "refrigerant" all read as properties, and a pipeline that scrapes for property words will happily convert an action into a humoral temperature. Three of 97 got that far this round. The same trap is still live inside eleven *confirmed* rows, most sharply at H001 Ashwagandha, where the word "hot" sits in a mixed list that also contains actions (tonic, alterative) and tastes (pungent, astringent). Only "hot" may be read as thermal. Nothing else in that list may be converted into temperature or moisture.
